<header class="tour-header">

  <h1>24 Fruit Trees in a Tiny Phoenix Backyard Food Forest</h1>

  <div class="tour-categories">

    <span class="tour-category">Arizona</span>

    <span class="tour-category">Phoenix</span>

    <span class="tour-category">Food Forest Tours</span>

  <p class="tour-description">
    Tour Kim’s compact Phoenix food forest, where fruit trees, tropical plants,
    flowers, groundcovers, shade plants, and a backyard pond are packed into a
    surprisingly small residential growing space.
  </p>

  <div class="tour-meta">

    <div>
      <span class="meta-label">Host</span>
      <span class="meta-value">Kim</span>
    </div>

    <div>
      <span class="meta-label">Published</span>
      <span class="meta-value">August 28, 2026</span>
    </div>

  </div>

</header>


<p class="tour-lead">
Kim’s Phoenix garden is proof that an abundant edible landscape does not
require a huge property. Despite having only about 110 feet by 11 feet of
plantable space, she has managed to fit 24 fruit trees into the property while
also growing tropical ornamentals, vines, flowering plants, edible
groundcovers, and support plants. The result is a constantly evolving
small-space food forest shaped around Phoenix heat, afternoon shade, wind,
limited room, and the plants Kim simply enjoys growing.
</p>

<section class="tour-section">

<h2>Inside a Tiny Phoenix Food Forest</h2>

<p>
Kim’s garden is built around one major limitation: space. The property is a
corner lot, the backyard includes a large swimming pool, and much of the
remaining plantable area consists of relatively narrow strips around the home.
Instead of treating that as a reason to keep the landscape simple, Kim has
used nearly every available pocket to grow something.
</p>

<p>
Fruit trees are tucked beside walls, near the pool, along the sides of the
house, around the pond, and into the front yard. Containers add another layer
where planting directly in the ground is not practical. Tropical ornamentals,
flowering shrubs, vines, edible groundcovers, and temporary shade plants fill
the spaces between the permanent trees.
</p>

<p>
The biggest surprise comes near the end of the tour, when Kim counts 24 fruit
trees on the property. That number becomes even more impressive when she
estimates that the usable planting area is only about 110 feet long by 11 feet
wide. This is not abundance created by owning more land. It is abundance
created by continually finding better ways to use the land that is available.
</p>

</section>


<section class="tour-section">

<h2>What You’ll Learn From Kim’s Phoenix Food Forest</h2>

<div class="learn-grid">

  <div class="learn-item">
    How Kim fits 24 fruit trees into a property with only about
    110 × 11 feet of practical planting space
  </div>

  <div class="learn-item">
    Why the east side of a Phoenix home can become valuable growing space
    for tropical plants that benefit from afternoon shade
  </div>

  <div class="learn-item">
    How pruning and intentionally keeping trees small can make a dense
    backyard orchard easier to manage
  </div>

  <div class="learn-item">
    How seasonal vines, castor bean, bamboo, and permanent trees can all
    contribute to summer shade and microclimates
  </div>

  <div class="learn-item">
    How Kim uses plants for multiple purposes, including fruit, privacy,
    shade, soil cover, flowers, and pollinator habitat
  </div>

  <div class="learn-item">
    Why a productive garden can still be a work in progress, with trees
    recovering, being moved, replaced, or redesigned as the gardener changes
  </div>

</div>

</section>

<section class="tour-section">

<h2>Designing Around Phoenix Heat and Afternoon Sun</h2>

<p>
One of the most useful parts of Kim’s tour is seeing how differently she treats
each exposure around the house. Her corner lot receives intense sun and wind,
and the western exposure can be especially difficult. The east side, however,
becomes a valuable microclimate because the house begins shading it during the
hottest part of summer afternoons.
</p>

<p>
Kim uses that protected side for many of her more tropical plants. The goal is
not to eliminate Arizona heat, but to control when the plants receive it.
Morning sun can provide plenty of light while afternoon shade reduces the
intensity of the hottest June, July, and August conditions.
</p>

<p>
She also creates temporary shade rather than relying only on permanent
structures. Fast-growing castor bean can provide seasonal protection. Vines
cover the pergola during summer, shading mango trees below, and can then be
removed when winter arrives so those same trees receive more sun.
</p>

<p>
Bamboo on the west side of the pergola adds another layer of protection,
blocking late-afternoon sunlight that could still reach the mangoes after the
overhead shade was in place. The garden shows how a small property can contain
many different microclimates simply by paying attention to walls, structures,
sun angles, and neighboring plants.
</p>

</section>


<section class="tour-section">

<h2>Keeping Fruit Trees Small on Purpose</h2>

<p>
A collection of 24 fruit trees would be difficult to maintain in this amount
of space if every tree were allowed to reach its natural mature size. Kim
instead treats pruning as part of the design. Several trees are deliberately
kept compact so they remain compatible with the house, pool, walkways, and
neighboring plants.
</p>

<p>
Her Pakistan mulberry is a good example of what happens when a vigorous tree
outgrows the role available to it. Kim has repeatedly removed several feet of
growth, yet the tree continues expanding rapidly. During the tour she explains
that it may ultimately need to leave because it simply wants more space than
the property can comfortably provide.
</p>

<p>
Other trees fit the system better when kept small. The limequat can be pruned
within reach. White sapote, guava, citrus, Barbados cherry, mango, and other
fruit trees are managed at a scale that makes sense for a residential yard.
The goal is not to see how large each tree can become. It is to keep many
different trees productive within the same limited landscape.
</p>

</section>


<section class="tour-section">

<h2>Growing Diversity in a Small Phoenix Backyard</h2>

<p>
Kim’s collection shows how much variety can fit into a small residential
landscape when every planting area is used intentionally. Mangoes, limequat,
longan, starfruit, white sapote, guavas, citrus, Barbados cherry, peach,
mulberry, papaya, and other fruit trees occupy narrow strips beside the house,
the front yard, and spaces around the backyard.
</p>

<p>
Many plants also serve more than one purpose. Fruit trees can shade the house,
bamboo and seasonal vines protect tropical plants from intense afternoon sun,
sweet potato covers exposed soil, and flowering plants add beauty and
pollinator habitat. The pond, which grew larger as Kim discovered how much she
enjoyed it, now provides a focal point and nutrient-rich water for nearby
mangoes.
</p>

<p>
Kim also describes the property as a “recovery yard.” Some plants declined
during a period when the garden received less attention, and several are now
recovering or being reconsidered. That ongoing process is part of the story:
the food forest continues to change as Kim learns which plants, locations, and
design choices work best for her limited Phoenix space.
</p>

</section>


<section class="tour-section">

<h2>Plants Growing in Kim’s Phoenix Food Forest</h2>

<p>
Kim’s small property contains an unusually broad collection of fruit trees,
tropical ornamentals, flowering plants, vines, groundcovers, and support
plants. Some are permanent parts of the food forest, while others are used
temporarily for shade or are still being evaluated as the garden evolves.
</p>

<section class="tour-section">

<h2>The Green Yard Takeaway</h2>

<div class="takeaway">

<p>
Kim’s garden demonstrates that abundance is not simply a matter of owning more
land. With roughly 110 feet by 11 feet of plantable space, she has managed to
fit 24 fruit trees into the property while still making room for tropical
plants, flowers, vines, groundcovers, a swimming pool, and a pond.
</p>

<p>
The bigger lesson is how she uses that limited space. Trees are kept small,
afternoon shade is treated as a resource, temporary plants create seasonal
microclimates, and individual plants often perform several jobs at once. Even
the parts of the garden that are recovering or changing become part of the
story. Kim’s yard shows that a small edible landscape can still hold enormous
diversity when the gardener is willing to experiment and continually adapt.
</p>

</div>

</section>
